title: Deterministic NP-hardness reductions for Euclidean SVP
formal:
Is the exact decision version of the Euclidean shortest vector problem NP-hard under a uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction?

An instance consists of a positive integer \(n\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), and a positive rational squared-radius threshold \(b\), all explicitly encoded in binary as specified below. Its lattice and Euclidean minimum are
\[
L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^{n}\},\qquad
\lambda_{1}(L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^{n}\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_{2},
\qquad \|x\|_{2}=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{2}\right)^{1/2}.
\]
The answer is YES if \(\lambda_{1}(L(B))^{2}\le b\), and NO if \(\lambda_{1}(L(B))^{2}>b\). Thus the geometric radius is \(\sqrt{b}\), represented exactly by its rational square.

Precisely, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(M\) and integers \(a,k\ge1\) such that, on every encoded 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\), it outputs a valid instance \((B_{\varphi},b_{\varphi})\) within \(a(|\varphi|+1)^{k}\) steps and
\[
\varphi\text{ is satisfiable}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\mathbb Z^{n_{\varphi}}\setminus\{0\}\quad
\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\varphi}}(B_{\varphi}z)_{i}^{2}\le b_{\varphi}?
\]
The same machine and constants must work for every input length. It must have the same time bound on malformed input strings, mapping them to valid NO instances.

This is the exact endpoint \(\gamma=1\) expressly allowed by the source's request for hardness of exact or approximate GapSVP under a deterministic Karp reduction. No approximation factor greater than one is required; a valid stronger gap reduction would also settle this endpoint.
why: The shortest vector problem is a central lattice problem whose basic hardness theorem historically required randomized reductions. Removing randomness establishes its ordinary NP-hardness and separates the foundational exact worst-case question from approximation regimes and average-case assumptions used in lattice cryptography.
status_note: Bennett explicitly posed this exact-or-approximate deterministic Karp-hardness question in January 2023. Wan’s arXiv 2603.27398v3 (22 July 2026) states a positive solution covering exact Euclidean GapSVP, and Hirahara–Ogitsuka’s 9 September 2026 conference paper independently describes that range as unconditional deterministic polynomial-time many-one hardness. The present review checked the matching theorem, explicit construction, projection argument, parameter and reduction-time chain, and key stated arithmetic dependencies; it did not formally verify the full proof or reconstruct its underlying cohomology. Wan’s work is a preprint in the checked record. The separate August preprint’s corrected tensor argument is not needed for this exact endpoint. This review supports a resolved disposition for the original exact endpoint, subject to the stated proof-audit limits; it does not assert peer-reviewed publication of the underlying hardness manuscript.

progress.text: Bennett’s survey defines rational-basis decision and search versions separately and poses deterministic Karp NP-hardness of exact or approximate Euclidean GapSVP as Open Problem 2.1. Exact hardness is expressly sufficient.

Bennett and Peikert give an explicit transfer theorem: a deterministic polynomial-time construction of the specified locally dense lattice yields deterministic NP-hardness for the corresponding approximation range. Their unconditional construction in that paper uses randomness.

Hair and Sahai give deterministic hardness in every fixed finite norm through reductions of subexponential size and running time. Their theorem uses a stronger deterministic subexponential-time complexity assumption and does not itself provide a polynomial-time Karp reduction.

Wan’s third arXiv version states that \(\gamma\)-GapSVP in every fixed finite \(\ell_{p}\) norm is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time reductions for \(1\le\gamma<2^{1/p}\). Setting \(p=2\) and \(\gamma=1\) matches this card; the result remains a preprint in the checked record.

Wan’s separate approximation preprint is revised to claim deterministic polynomial-time Euclidean hardness for every fixed factor. It explicitly replaces an incorrect tensor argument in its first version and no longer retains that version’s dimension-dependent claims; the exact-endpoint result comes from the earlier paper and does not depend on that tensor argument.

Hirahara and Ogitsuka’s published APPROX/RANDOM paper explicitly cites Wan’s below-square-root-of-two range as unconditional deterministic polynomial-time many-one hardness. Their own extension to all constant factors assumes a nondeterministic-circuit lower bound.

sentences: Euclidean SVP asks whether a lattice contains a nonzero vector within an explicitly given radius.
The source asks for a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction proving NP-hardness and explicitly allows the exact decision version.
This formulation fixes rational full-rank bases, rational squared radii, binary encodings and a uniform bit-cost machine, without an extra approximation gap or complexity assumption.
Wan’s 2026 preprint states a matching positive result, and an independent September conference paper recognizes its deterministic polynomial-time hardness range.
The recorded proof-chain review supports resolution of the original exact target, while keeping its limits and the preprint status explicit.

definitions:
A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of exactly three literals; a literal is a Boolean variable or its negation. Variables have positive integer labels, and labels or literals may repeat. An assignment maps the finitely many labels occurring in the formula to \(\{0,1\}\); a positive literal is true when its variable is one, and a negative literal when its variable is zero. A clause is true if at least one literal is true, and the formula is true if every clause is true. The conjunction of zero clauses is true.

Fix the finite input alphabet \(\Sigma=\{0,1,+,-,(,),\texttt{,}\}\). A literal is a sign followed by the usual binary representation of a positive integer, without leading zeros. A clause consists of an opening parenthesis, three such literals separated by commas, and a closing parenthesis. An encoded formula is a concatenation of zero or more clauses; no whitespace is used. The empty string encodes the empty conjunction. All other strings over \(\Sigma\) are malformed. Let \(\mathrm{SAT}_{3}(s)\) mean that \(s\) is a well-formed formula with a satisfying assignment, and let this predicate be false for malformed strings. The input length \(|s|\) is the number of symbols in this encoding; integer labels are represented explicitly, not by unit-cost integers or a separate count of unused variables.

For lattice output, an integer is represented by a sign and its binary magnitude, without leading zeros; zero has the representation \(+0\). A rational is represented by a numerator and a strictly positive denominator in lowest terms, separated by \(\texttt{/}\); its zero numerator is therefore paired with denominator one. The output is the binary dimension \(n\ge1\), followed by the \(n^{2}\) entries of \(B\) in row-major order, followed by \(b\), with consecutive fields separated by \(\texttt{;}\). The dimension has no leading zeros. The numerator uses the signed integer encoding, and denominators use unsigned positive binary encoding. The complete output contains exactly the indicated number of fields. Validity requires \(\det B\ne0\) and \(b>0\). This provides a finite exact representation of every allowed rational full-rank basis and squared-radius threshold; the reduction must print the whole representation.

The rational basis vectors are the columns of \(B\), and their integer span defines \(L(B)\). Nonsingularity ensures that \(Bz\ne0\) exactly when \(z\ne0\), and that the lattice has a positive attained minimum. The input basis need not be reduced, orthogonal, triangular, or short. There is no uniqueness promise for a shortest vector and no restriction on the determinant, entries, or dimension beyond their explicit encoding and the reduction's polynomial output bound. The norm is the ordinary Euclidean norm of the specified coordinates. All comparisons in the decision predicate use the rational number \(b\) and squared rational coordinates; no rounding or unit-cost real arithmetic is allowed. Storing a rational square permits an irrational geometric radius, such as the square root of an integer, without any ambiguity.

A deterministic machine is an ordinary multitape Turing machine with a finite control, a fixed finite tape alphabet containing the encoding symbols, a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes, and an output tape. Every transition reads and writes at most one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. The initial state, blank symbol and initial head positions are fixed in its finite description. Input inspection, arithmetic on binary integers and fractions, and writing every output symbol count toward runtime. There are no random bits, advice strings, nondeterministic choices, oracle calls, quantum operations, or unit-cost operations on arbitrarily large numbers. The resource bound is worst-case total running time on every string. In particular, the output dimension and total bit length are automatically polynomially bounded in input length. Polynomial exponents and leading constants may depend on the single chosen machine, but not on the input length or formula.

A Karp reduction is a many-one reduction: the machine produces one instance, whose one YES/NO answer decides the original membership question. It does not make adaptive queries to a shortest-vector oracle and need not compute a shortest vector or a satisfying assignment. Using the fixed NP-complete source language \(\mathrm{SAT}_{3}\) is equivalent to NP-hardness under this reduction type. Here NP consists of languages whose YES membership has polynomial-length certificates checkable by a deterministic polynomial-time machine. NP-hardness is the unconditional reduction assertion; the target does not assume \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), an exponential-time hypothesis, or a circuit lower bound.

For completeness, the source defines \(\gamma\)-GapSVP, for \(\gamma\ge1\), by the promise that either \(\lambda_{1}(L(B))\le r\) or \(\lambda_{1}(L(B))>\gamma r\). In this card's encoding \(r=\sqrt{b}\), so these conditions become \(\lambda_{1}(L(B))^{2}\le b\) and \(\lambda_{1}(L(B))^{2}>\gamma^{2}b\). At \(\gamma=1\), every valid instance meets exactly one of the two conditions, so the selected problem is an ordinary decision problem with no missing interval. The word Gap in the source's name distinguishes decision from search and does not itself impose a gap larger than one. The card keeps the source's Euclidean norm and exact endpoint. Storing the squared radius is an explicit finite-encoding convention, polynomial-time equivalent for rational-basis exact SVP to a rational-radius encoding; it does not impose a stronger approximation theorem or a numerical tolerance.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence assertion in the formal statement or of its logical negation.

For a finite deterministic machine description \(M\), positive integers \(a,k\), and a string \(s\in\Sigma^{*}\), define \(\mathrm{Good}(M,a,k,s)\) to mean that the run halts within \(a(|s|+1)^{k}\) steps, prints exactly one valid encoded rational full-rank lattice instance \((B,b)\), and satisfies
\[
\mathrm{SAT}_{3}(s)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\mathbb Z^{n}\setminus\{0\}\quad
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Bz)_{i}^{2}\le b.
\]
Thus the affirmative theorem is
\[
\exists M\;\exists a,k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\;\forall s\in\Sigma^{*},
\quad\mathrm{Good}(M,a,k,s).
\]
A positive solution must prove deterministic uniform construction, the total bit-cost runtime bound, output validity, and both the satisfiable and unsatisfiable cases, for all strings. No separate assumption about \(\mathrm{P}\), \(\mathrm{NP}\), randomness, or cryptographic hardness is allowed.

The negative theorem is the full negation
\[
\forall M\;\forall a,k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\;\exists s\in\Sigma^{*},
\quad\neg\mathrm{Good}(M,a,k,s).
\]
It must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction in the stated model, allowing the failed input to depend on the machine and its proposed time bound. A failure of one construction, an oracle separation, or a limitation on a special reduction framework does not establish this negation. A randomized reduction, a nonuniform family, a deterministic superpolynomial-time reduction, hardness only in a different norm, or a conditional hardness theorem does not establish the positive assertion. There is no numerical tolerance on the exact YES/NO equivalence or the polynomial-time guarantee.

context_blocks.text: Bennett’s 2023 Open Problem 2.1 explicitly permits exact Euclidean GapSVP and asks for a deterministic Karp reduction.
The exact endpoint is a decision problem about whether a nonzero lattice vector lies within a given radius, with no approximation interval left unspecified.
Earlier randomized hardness and deterministic results with superpolynomial reduction time do not by themselves establish the unconditional polynomial-time reduction asked for here.

Wan’s 2026 preprint states deterministic polynomial-time hardness for every factor below the square root of two, including this exact endpoint, and its July revision supplies the complete projection argument.

A September 2026 conference paper independently describes that exact-range result as unconditional, while the present review records the preprint’s publication status and the limits of its proof audit.

checked_sources: Read full canonical data/cards/TCS-0651.json and docs/RULES.md. Existing score 85 was already individually assessed; this draft intentionally contains no replacement importance field. Downloaded original 25-page svp-color.pdf to sources/svp-det-gasarch.pdf/.txt. Read Definitions 1.1–1.2 PDF 4, exact convention and footnote 3 PDF 5, full Open Problem 2.1 and surrounding paragraphs PDF 6. Exact OR approximate Euclidean GapSVP under deterministic Karp is the literal source target. The exact gamma = 1 endpoint is faithful, not a newly narrowed approximation threshold. Source version24 January 2023; no dependence on 2026 publicity.

Encoding precision: original definition uses a nonsingular square rational basis. Retained that model, positive rational squared-radius threshold, finite explicit binary representations, standard deterministic multitape bit cost, uniform machine, no advice/oracle/randomness and a single many-one output. The source permits more general rectangular bases in footnote 2 but does not require those. The exact decision predicate compares squared rational lengths with a rational squared radius and needs no real-arithmetic oracle. 3SAT with literal repetitions remains NP-complete, and malformed strings are mapped to NO so the entire machine domain is specified. Affirmative and negative Lean quantifiers are complete; a negative answer means every machine and every proposed polynomial bound has a failing input, not failure of a particular method.

Squared-radius equivalence audit: for a rational basis B, let D be the product of its positive entry denominators, so C=DB is integral and ||Cz||_2^2 is an integer. Rational radius r maps to b=r^2 directly. Conversely, given positive rational squared radius b, put K=floor(D^2 b), S=4(K+1), U=floor(sqrt(K S^2))+1 and r=U/(SD). Exact integer square root is polynomial-time. Then K<U^2/S^2<K+1, since 2sqrt(K)/S+1/S^2<1, including K=0. Consequently ||Bz||_2^2<=b iff ||Bz||_2<=r for every integer z. All constructed integers and fractions have polynomial bit length. Thus the card represents natural reduction thresholds such as sqrt(integer) exactly without changing the exact source problem. Tracked substantive audit: research/random-card-review-20260914/tcs-0651-svp-proof-audit.md.

Main matching paper: sources/svp-det-wanbase2026.pdf/.txt is actual arXiv 2603.27398v3, 29 pages. Metadata: v1 28 March 2026, v2 15 July 2026, v3 22 July 2026; PDF dated 23 July. Read entire substantive chain: Problem 1.5 PDF 3, Theorem 1.8 PDF 5, Definition 2.1/Theorem 2.2 PDF 7, explicit basis Proposition 3.2 PDF 9, lower-bound Lemma 3.4 PDF 10, coset definitions PDF 11–13, complete-intersection and smoothness Propositions 4.2/4.4 PDF 14–17, point-counting Propositions 5.1–5.3 PDF 17–19, collision exclusion and density PDF 20–23, complete projection proof Section 7 PDF 24–28, Theorem 7.3 PDF 27 and Theorem 7.4 PDF 28. These explicitly include p2 and gamma = 1 with deterministic polynomial construction; no SAT hardness assumption is added. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.27398v3

Proof audit, not public solver guidance: Wan constructs the Reed–Solomon congruence lattice using a block integer basis with entries bounded by q; the center is a fixed constant-weight binary vector and the projection uses the first r coordinates. Surjectivity for every binary pattern is proved via a uniform point count plus exclusions, not by algorithmically enumerating all patterns. The reduction need not find a satisfying lattice witness. Fixed rational epsilon,epsilon1,delta with delta<epsilon1 give q polynomial in the source rank. PDF 28 explicitly scans a polynomial-size interval for a prime and uses a deterministic primality test; finite small cases are absorbed by a fixed cutoff. No nonuniform good seed or exponential construction was found in this portion.

Arithmetic audit: Proposition 4.4 PDF 16 uses the invertible Vandermonde matrix and positive multiplicities below the prime to show smoothness at infinity. With Proposition 4.2, the singularities of the projective closure are at most isolated; Proposition 5.1 supplies the Deligne–Hooley–Katz extension-field point-count exponent. Proposition 5.2 obtains a uniform error constant via the rational zeta function and an affine Betti bound. The later collision and prescribed-coordinate exclusions preserve positive main terms for the stated fixed exponents. I checked the stated hypotheses and arithmetic use, but did not independently rebuild the full cohomological theorem or certify the proof in Lean. No fatal issue was identified in this bounded audit.

External arithmetic statements checked in actual primary files: sources/svp-det-katz1999.pdf/.txt from https://web.math.princeton.edu/~nmk/ESES.pdf, Nicholas Katz, Estimates for Singular Exponential Sums (1999), Lemma 3 printed878/PDF 4 proves the singular-dimension inequality used for the closure. sources/svp-det-bettibounds.pdf/.txt from https://zhangdingxin.gitlab.io/math/pdf/betti.pdf, Wan–Zhang, Betti number bounds for varieties and exponential sums, Advances in Mathematics490(2026)110852, DOI10.1016/j.aim.2026.110852, Theorem 1.2.1 PDF 5 gives Bc≤binomial(n−1,r−1)(d+1)^n for affine complete intersections of the stated codimension; it matches Wan’s substitution. The source cites this once with a different theorem number, but the actual bound is present. These dependencies are not asserted to be original to the hardness paper.

Transfer checked in actual publisher PDF sources/svp-det-bennettpeikert2023.pdf/.txt. Bennett–Peikert APPROX/RANDOM 2023 article 37: Theorem 12 / Corollary 13 PDF 12 explicitly state deterministic polynomial hardness when the locally dense lattice is constructed deterministically, with projection condition in Definition 8. Thus the interface is not merely a randomized or nonuniform reduction. https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.APPROX/RANDOM.2023.37

Square-basis model bridge, kept in audit rather than public hints: the published transfer can output a full-column-rank rectangular integer matrix B. It has a deterministic polynomial-time conversion to a square integer basis without changing a fixed-radius decision. Compute an integer basis C for the rational orthogonal complement of B by exact Gaussian elimination and clearing denominators. Set M=ceil(b)+1, which is strictly greater than sqrt(b) for every b>0. Then D=[B,MC] is square and nonsingular; every nonzero C component has squared norm at least M^2 because C has integer entries and independent columns, and is orthogonal to B. Hence vectors of squared norm at most b in L(D) are exactly the original short vectors. Rational squared threshold and matrix bit lengths stay polynomial. The card’s square model therefore does not create a missing restriction in the cited hardness target.
